topic: the concept of a chemical reaction's reactants determining possible products

easy.text: In a chemical reaction, what determines the elements that can appear in the products?

options.text: The elements that were present in the reactants -- no new elements can be created in a normal chemical reaction
options.feedback: Correct -- chemical reactions only rearrange existing atoms into new combinations; they don't create or destroy elements.

options.text: Any element the chemist wants can simply appear in the products
options.feedback: This isn't correct -- ordinary chemical reactions can't introduce entirely new elements not already present in the reactants.

options.text: Products always contain completely different elements from the reactants
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- products are made of the SAME elements originally present in the reactants, just rearranged into new combinations.

options.text: Only reactions involving oxygen can determine product elements
options.feedback: This applies to all chemical reactions generally, not something unique to reactions specifically involving oxygen.

medium.text: If a reaction starts with only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms, why is it impossible for one of the products to contain nitrogen?

options.text: Chemical reactions cannot create new elements -- nitrogen atoms would have to already be present in the reactants for them to appear in a product
options.feedback: Correct -- this reflects the fundamental principle of conservation of elements/mass in chemical reactions.

options.text: Nitrogen atoms can spontaneously appear during any chemical reaction
options.feedback: This isn't possible under normal chemical reactions -- elements are conserved, not created, during typical chemistry.

options.text: This is actually possible and happens routinely in chemical reactions
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- ordinary chemical reactions cannot create entirely new elements not present among the original reactants.

options.text: Nitrogen is a special element that follows completely different rules
options.feedback: Nitrogen follows the same fundamental principle as every other element -- reactions can't create elements not already present in the reactants.

hard.text: Nuclear reactions, unlike ordinary chemical reactions, CAN actually transform one element into a different element entirely. Why does this fundamental distinction exist between chemical and nuclear processes?

options.text: Chemical reactions only involve rearranging electrons and bonds between atoms, while nuclear reactions involve changes within the atomic nucleus itself (protons/neutrons), which is what actually determines an element's identity
options.feedback: Correct -- since an element's identity is defined by its number of protons, only a nuclear-level change (unlike ordinary electron-based chemical bonding) can transform one element into another.

options.text: There is actually no real distinction between chemical and nuclear reactions
options.feedback: There is a very real, fundamental distinction -- chemical reactions involve electron rearrangement, while nuclear reactions involve changes to the nucleus itself, which is why only nuclear reactions can transmute elements.

options.text: Chemical reactions actually can transform elements just as easily as nuclear reactions
options.feedback: This is incorrect -- ordinary chemical reactions cannot change one element into another; that specifically requires a nuclear-level process.

options.text: Nuclear reactions don't actually involve atoms at all
options.feedback: Nuclear reactions definitely involve atoms -- specifically, changes occurring within their nuclei, which is the key distinguishing feature from ordinary chemical reactions.

easy.hard: Chemical reactions rearrange existing atomic building blocks rather than creating entirely new ones.
easy.medium: A chemical reaction can only rearrange atoms that were already there to begin with.
easy.easy: A chemical reaction can only rearrange the atoms that were already there.

medium.hard: Consider the fundamental principle that chemical processes conserve the identity and quantity of every element present throughout the reaction.
medium.medium: Since nitrogen wasn't part of the starting materials, there's no way for it to just show up in the products.
medium.easy: Since nitrogen wasn't in the starting materials, it can't just show up in the products.

hard.hard: An element's identity is defined specifically by its proton count, which chemical (electron-level) reactions cannot alter -- only nuclear-level processes affecting the proton count can transmute one element into another.
hard.medium: Chemical reactions only mess with the outer electrons, but changing what element something IS requires actually changing its nucleus, which only nuclear reactions can do.
hard.easy: Chemical reactions only mess with outer electrons, but changing what element something is requires changing its nucleus.
